children: CVS Health has decided to split in two, reversing one of the signature deals that defined an era of health industry gigantism.
One company will house its insurance giant Aetna and pharmacy-benefit manager Caremark, the other its 9,000 retail pharmacies.

The breakup, planned for early 2028, comes a decade after the near-$70 billion merger that knit together Aetna and CVS, creating one of a new breed of giants that brought together multiple businesses spanning more of the healthcare industry.

Now, CVS says, the businesses will be better off on their own. "We believe based off of where we are and how we're performing, the businesses are best served by splitting," said CVS Chief Executive David Joyner. "We're basically taking what I believe is one great company and making it two."

Joyner said the breakup will enable the two separate management teams to focus more on their respective businesses and be more agile. The company has turned around Aetna and bolstered its retail performance, he said, enabling it to make this change from a position of strength.

Healthcare giants such as CVS, which integrate an array of intertwined businesses, are coming under growing pressure from federal and state-level regulators and lawmakers. The scrutiny may intensify if Democrats achieve congressional majorities in the House or Senate, but the pressure has been bipartisan. Republicans in Tennessee and Arkansas have passed laws — challenged in court by CVS and other firms — that would ban co-ownership of pharmacies and pharmacy-benefit managers, or PBMs. Joyner said the company wasn't making the change because of regulatory issues.
After CVS's split, the two resulting companies will both be publicly traded, and current shareholders will own shares in both.

One of the two new firms will keep the CVS Health name, and will be run by Joyner. In addition to the insurance and PBM assets, that company will include Oak Street Health's senior clinics, the home-visit provider Signify Health, and CVS's specialty-drug business, a key growth driver.

The other new company, to be dubbed CVS Pharmacy, will own mail-order pharmacy, the retail drugstores, their associated MinuteClinic providers, and Health100, a consumer-focused digital tool powered by artificial intelligence.

The pharmacy company will be forced to grapple with long-running challenges in the retail drugstore business, without the protection of its PBM and insurance units. CVS's big pharmacy competitor, Walgreens, went private last year after struggling to regain momentum.

Joyner said that CVS Pharmacy, which has been gaining market share and stabilizing its margins in recent quarters, is positioned to be a strong stand-alone firm, after changes including trimming underperforming stores and creating Health100 as a consumer destination.

On the other side, he said, putting together Aetna with Caremark makes sense because of synergies in the two units that manage health and drug benefits. The senior-focused assets will help bolster Aetna's key Medicare business, he said.
The two CVS firms will be tied together with a commercial agreement that will preserve "some products and services that actually make the companies unique," Joyner said.
The Financial Times earlier on Tuesday reported the breakup.
